questions.topic: Rediscovering the Roots of Atomic Theory
questions.stem: Nisha is preparing a class display on how the idea of the atom first arose, and she wonders why it appeared so long before anyone could test it in a laboratory. Consider the following statements. 1. The idea that matter is made up of particles which cannot be divided any further was put forward in ancient India and ancient Greece, many centuries before it rested on experimental evidence. 2. The thinkers of both civilisations arrived at that idea by pondering what everything is made up of, and not by carrying out experiments. Choose the correct option. (A) Both the assertion and the reason are true and the reason is a correct explanation of the assertion. (B) Both the assertion and the reason are true but the reason is not a correct explanation of the assertion. (C) The assertion is true but the reason is false. (D) Both the assertion and the reason are false.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: Both the assertion and the reason are true and the reason is a correct explanation of the assertion.

questions.stem: A student is asked whether a claim about matter belongs to the age of experiments or to the age of pure thought, and points out that one account of matter was put forward in 1808 and became the starting point for all later work on atomic structure. Consider the following statements. 1. The atomic theory proposed by John Dalton in 1808 was the first scientific description of how matter is made. 2. Dalton arrived at that theory by following Acharya Kanada's method of dividing matter repeatedly until particles that can no longer be divided are reached, instead of relying on experiments. Choose the correct option. (A) Both the assertion and the reason are true and the reason is a correct explanation of the assertion. (B) Both the assertion and the reason are true but the reason is not a correct explanation of the assertion. (C) The assertion is true but the reason is false. (D) Both the assertion and the reason are false.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: The assertion is true but the reason is false.
